question: Define the three ANSI SQL read phenomena: Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, and Phantom Read.? Define the three ANSI SQL read phenomena: Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, and Phantom Read.

options.text: Dirty Read: reading uncommitted changes; Non-Repeatable Read: re-reading a row returns modified values; Phantom Read: re-executing range query returns newly inserted rows.
Dirty Read: re-reading a row returns modified values; Non-Repeatable Read: reading uncommitted changes; Phantom Read: reading a row that was deleted by another transaction.
Dirty Read and Non-Repeatable Read are the same phenomenon under different names; Phantom Read only occurs in single-row queries, never in range queries.
Phantom Read: reading uncommitted changes from another transaction that later rolls back; Dirty Read: a range query returns a different set of rows on re-execution.

explanation: Specification answer: Dirty Read: reading uncommitted changes; Non-Repeatable Read: re-reading a row returns modified values; Phantom Read: re-executing range query returns newly inserted rows.

question: What is the difference between Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Strict 2PL (S2PL)? What is the difference between Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Strict 2PL (S2PL)?

options.text: 2PL releases locks during shrinking phase before commit; Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until transaction COMMIT or ABORT, preventing cascading rollbacks.
2PL holds all locks until commit or abort, while Strict 2PL allows releasing locks during a shrinking phase before the transaction ends.
Strict 2PL only applies to read locks, releasing write locks immediately after each statement, while plain 2PL holds both lock types until commit.
2PL and Strict 2PL differ only in how many locks a transaction may hold simultaneously, not in when those locks are released.

explanation: Specification answer: 2PL releases locks during shrinking phase before commit; Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until transaction COMMIT or ABORT, preventing cascading rollbacks.

question: Explain the two phases of the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol.? Explain the two phases of the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol.

options.text: Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator asks participants if they can commit; participants vote YES and write to WAL. Phase 2 (Commit): If all voted YES, coordinator issues COMMIT; otherwise ABORT.
Phase 1 (Commit): the coordinator immediately applies the transaction on all participants. Phase 2 (Prepare): participants confirm afterward that the already-applied changes were valid.
Phase 1: each participant independently decides to commit or abort without consulting the coordinator. Phase 2: the coordinator only logs the outcome for audit purposes.
Phase 1 (Prepare): the coordinator commits its own local changes first. Phase 2 (Vote): participants then vote on whether to accept the coordinator's already-committed state.

explanation: Specification answer: Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator asks participants if they can commit; participants vote YES and write to WAL. Phase 2 (Commit): If all voted YES, coordinator issues COMMIT; otherwise ABORT.

question: Why is 2PC considered a blocking protocol? Why is 2PC considered a blocking protocol?

options.text: If the coordinator crashes after participants enter the PREPARED state, participants must hold locks indefinitely until coordinator recovers.
2PC is blocking because every participant must communicate directly with every other participant during the prepare phase, creating an all-to-all network bottleneck.
2PC is blocking only when participants use pessimistic locking; participants using optimistic concurrency control never block, even if the coordinator crashes.
A participant that voted NO in the prepare phase is blocked from starting any new transaction until the coordinator explicitly sends it an ABORT for the current one.

explanation: Specification answer: If the coordinator crashes after participants enter the PREPARED state, participants must hold locks indefinitely until coordinator recovers.

question:
During triage in Transactions Isolation Consensus Raft, an engineer observes:
"System fault during operation: Split-Brain Dual Leader Election in Raft Cluster".
What is the verified root cause?

options.text: Candidate node transitions to Leader after receiving 2 votes in a 5-node cluster, violating majority quorum ($N/2 + 1 = 3$).

The candidate correctly waited for a majority of 3 votes, but two of the five nodes were partitioned from each other and each formed their own valid majority within their partition, so two leaders emerged simultaneously despite correct vote counting.

votes_received counts the candidate's own vote twice, once at self-vote and once when its RequestVote reply arrives back over the network, so 2 real votes from other nodes are miscounted as reaching the majority of 3.
The cluster size was miscalculated as 3 instead of 5 because two nodes had not yet finished joining, so a majority of 2 out of the assumed 3-node cluster was treated as sufficient.

explanation:
Root Cause: Candidate node transitions to Leader after receiving 2 votes in a 5-node cluster, violating majority quorum ($N/2 + 1 = 3$).

Fix Resolution:
Require strict majority: if votesreceived >= (len(self.nodes) // 2) + 1: self.becomeleader().
